BEFORE CHAPTER ONE

How to say it

The book uses standard spoken Malayalam in Roman letters. Names keep their usual spelling. Try the line below, then use the guide whenever a sound is new.

njaan Rahul aanuh.I’m Rahul.

Vowels

a / aa
Roughly the vowel in “cup” and the longer “ah” in “father.”
i / ii
Short as in “bit,” long as in “see.”
u / uu
Short and long “oo.” Round your lips as in “food.”
e / ee
Start near “bed.” For the long sound, hold the start of “say” steady.
o / oo
Use the start of “go,” without the glide. Hold it longer for oo.
ai / au
Roughly “eye” and the “ow” in “now.”
uh
A quick, relaxed vowel like the start of “about.” Try the ending of aanuh.

Consonants to listen for

ch / cch / sh
“Chair,” a held version of that sound, and “ship.”
nj / ng
“Ny” in “canyon” and “ng” in “sing.” Try njaan.
zh
An r-like sound. Curl your tongue tip back for mazha (“rain”).
r / v
A quick tongue tap for r. For v, bring your lower lip toward your upper teeth.
kk / pp / ll
Hold a doubled consonant a little longer. In vellam (“water”), curl your tongue back for ll.
d / dh
Say the d in ende (“my”) like the d in “end,” at the ridge behind your teeth. For dh in idhuh (“this”) and endhaa? (“what?”), touch the back of your upper front teeth and release a quick d sound. The h marks tongue position.
nd
In unduh (“there is”), curl your tongue back for nd. Try saying ende, endhaa, and unduh slowly to feel the three tongue positions.
n / tt
Curl back for the n in aanuh and veenam, and the tt in veettil. Use the ridge behind your teeth for the tt in pattum.

Some familiar letters cover more than one tongue position. The notes call out those differences. Read words such as aanuh separately on the page, then let them flow together naturally when you speak.

THE REGULARS

Meet the cast

Rahul and Kirti are a couple. Rahul is friends with Kevin and Siddharth. Kirti is Kevin’s older sister, so you’ll hear him call her cheechi. Samay and Devika are dating. Samay is friends with Rahul and Siddharth.

RahulKirtiKevinSiddharthSamayDevika

The friends sometimes use nee with one another. That’s a familiar “you.” With someone you’ve just met, you can often leave “you” out and ask chaaya veenoo? (“Would you like tea?”).

VOLUME 01 REVIEW

Put it together

Say each line out loud before revealing the answer. Then try the scene again with your own plans.

Language references

Original dialogues and exercises. Grammar and sound references include Rodney F. Moag’s Malayalam course and reference grammar, R. E. Asher and T. C. Kumari’s Malayalam, and the University of Texas guides to spoken pronunciation and time expressions. This edition is ready for learner review and a native-speaker pass.
